Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette:
Kofi, a 37-year-old African American psychologist who lived alone and kept a careful, orderly apartment, had been assaulted several years earlier in a way that left him deeply unsettled in places other people took for granted. The rape had happened when he was alone with a man in a space where he could not easily leave, and what stayed with him most was the trapped quality of it: the sense that the room had become smaller, that the door and the walls had taken on a finality he had not been able to negotiate. In the months afterward, Kofi found that certain moments carried him back with immediate force. If he found himself in a locked or confined room, even briefly, his body tightened before he had fully registered why. At work, when a meeting room door clicked shut behind him, he would notice himself scanning the room and choosing a chair that kept him oriented to the exit. He especially disliked being alone with men, even in ordinary professional settings, because one-on-one proximity could make him feel abruptly exposed and uncertain of what might happen next. He also found that comments about sexual violence, whether in the news, in discussion with colleagues, or in a client’s story, could strike him with the force of recognition and leave him visibly unsettled, as if something private had been brought into the open without warning.

Over time, Kofi’s days became organized around staying ready. He described needing his back against a wall so he could see the whole room, and in restaurants, offices, and waiting areas he would quietly position himself that way as soon as possible. If he could not do that, he remained tense and watchful, tracking who was entering, who was standing behind him, and how close men were coming. He said he could not relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, because his mind would not permit him to fully let go of the possibility that something bad could happen without warning. Nights were difficult in a different but related way. When he went to bed, he had trouble falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, and he often lay awake listening to the building settle or to footsteps in the hallway, aware that his body did not trust the quiet. He would turn on and off the lights, check the locks more than once, and remain in a state of half-readiness that left him drained the next day. At work as a psychologist, he continued to function, but the strain showed in the way he navigated his environment. He became increasingly deliberate about scheduling and room choices, and he felt uneasy in spaces where he might be expected to sit with a man alone behind a closed door. He did not describe these adjustments as dramatic, only necessary, the practical routines of someone who had learned not to assume safety.

What troubled Kofi most, however, was the meaning he had come to attach to himself. He had come to believe that he had no future, not in any hopeful sense, because the assault had changed what kind of life seemed available to him. He spoke with a flat certainty that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, and this conviction sat alongside a persistent sense of humiliation that made him feel that others could somehow see what had happened just by looking at him. In public, he sometimes felt as though his face, posture, or silence were giving him away, and he found himself monitoring how he appeared to colleagues, acquaintances, and clients. Being perceived this way made social contact feel loaded and exposed, even when no one had said anything. As a single man, he had gradually withdrawn from possibilities for closeness, not because he did not want connection, but because closeness seemed to invite the kinds of vulnerability he no longer trusted himself to manage.

By the time he sought help, Kofi was exhausted by the effort of staying composed. The week before he made the appointment, he had been caught off guard by a discussion at work in which someone referenced sexual violence in a clinical context, and the conversation left him shaken for the rest of the day. Not long after, he found himself in a locked room with a male colleague during a routine professional meeting and spent the entire interaction focused on the door, his chair, and the distance between them. That evening he sat awake for hours, unable to settle enough to sleep. He came to treatment not because he believed the danger had returned in the same form, but because he could no longer tolerate living as though it might. What he wanted most was relief from the constant vigilance and from the conviction that his future had already been erased; what he feared most was that the assault had marked him in a way that would forever keep him from feeling at ease with other people, or with himself.
